column14: It is a pure element, not a compound

column16: Covalent — the low melting point and the non-conducting solution both point to molecules
column17: There is no way to tell from these two tests
column28: A high melting point and a solution that conducts are both signs of an ionic compound.

column9: Count the atoms of S in (NH₄)₂S. (Watch the parentheses.)

column9: Which has the LOWER melting point: CCl₄ or KBr?
column14: They melt at the same temperature
column28: CCl₄ is covalent (all nonmetals); KBr is ionic. Covalent compounds have lower melting points.

column9: Solid salt does not conduct electricity, but salt water does. Why?
column14: Solid salt has no ions at all
column15: Salt loses its ions when it dissolves
column16: In the solid the ions are locked in place; dissolved in water, they can move
column17: Water by itself is a great conductor
column28: Charges have to move to carry current. Ions are stuck in the solid but free to move once dissolved.
A subscript outside parentheses multiplies everything inside: 2 O and 2 H.

column9: What is the TOTAL number of atoms in Al₂(SO₄)₃?
column28: Al = 2. The 3 multiplies S and O: S = 1 × 3 = 3, O = 4 × 3 = 12. Total = 2 + 3 + 12 = 17.
